title.en: The Primary Clear Light at the Moment of Death

region.en: Deathbed of the dying one, anywhere in Tibet (symbolic pin at the Chikhai bardo, symbolic)
region.zh: 亡者臨終之榻（以「臨終中陰」為象徵定位）

texts.period: Bardo Thodol (Bar-do thos-grol, terma attributed to Padmasambhava, revealed as 'Liberation by Hearing on the After-Death Plane'); English translation by Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz, 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (Oxford University Press, 1927), Part I, Book I

texts.license: Public domain (English translation published 1927; US public domain since 2023)

summary.en: At the very instant the breath ceases, the dying one is set face to face with the Primary Clear Light: all things like the void and cloudless sky, the naked spotless intellect like a transparent vacuum without circumference or centre. The lama names the symptoms of death one by one - earth sinking into water, water into fire, fire into air - enforces the resolve to win Buddhahood for all beings, presses the arteries and turns the body to the lion's posture so the vital-force passes out through the Brahmanic aperture, and repeats the address until a yellowish liquid appears at the apertures; the ordinary man endures the swoon but three and a half days, the yogi but a finger-snap.
summary.zh: 氣息將絕之際，上師令亡者直面「根本明光」：萬象如晴空無雲，赤裸無垢之心如無邊無際之澄空。上師逐一生宣死相——地入水、水入火、火入風——促其發願為一切眾生成佛，按住喉側動脈、作獅子臥，令命力自梵穴而出；反覆誦示，直至體竅滲出黃液。常人昏沉三日半，瑜伽行者僅一彈指。

texts.canonical_translation: Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, English translation; ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Tibetan Book of the Dead, Oxford 1927 (public domain)

narrative.en:
It is best if the guru from whom the deceased received guiding instructions can be had; but if the guru cannot be obtained, then a brother of the Faith; or if the latter is also unobtainable, then a learned man of the same Faith; or, should all these be unobtainable, then a person who can read correctly and distinctly ought to read this many times over. Thereby the deceased will be put in mind of what he had previously heard of the setting-face-to-face and will at once come to recognize that Fundamental Light and undoubtedly obtain Liberation.

When the breathing is about to cease, it is best if the Transference hath been applied efficiently; if the application hath been inefficient, then address the deceased thus: 'O nobly-born, the time hath now come for thee to seek the Path in reality. Thy breathing is about to cease. Thy guru hath set thee face to face before with the Clear Light; and now thou art about to experience it in its Reality in the Bardo state, wherein all things are like the void and cloudless sky, and the naked, spotless intellect is like unto a transparent vacuum without circumference or centre. At this moment, know thou thyself; and abide in that state.' Having read this, repeat it many times in the ear of the person dying, even before the expiration hath ceased, so as to impress it on the mind of the dying one.

If the expiration is about to cease, turn the dying one over on the right side, which posture is called the Lying Posture of a Lion; the throbbing of the arteries on the right and left side of the throat is to be pressed. If the person dying be disposed to sleep, or if the deep sleep state advances, that should be arrested, and the arteries pressed gently but firmly, whereby the vital-force will not be able to return from the median-nerve and will be sure to pass out through the Brahmanic aperture. At this moment the first glimpsing of the Bardo of the Clear Light of Reality, which is the Infallible Mind of the Dharma-Kaya, is experienced by all sentient beings. The interval between the cessation of the expiration and the cessation of the inspiration is the time during which the vital-force remaineth in the median-nerve. The common people call this the state wherein the consciousness-principle hath fainted away; the duration is uncertain, depending upon constitution, good or bad, and the state of the nerves and vital-force.

In the setting-face-to-face the repetition is to be persisted in until a yellowish liquid beginneth to appear from the various apertures of the bodily organs. In those who have led an evil life and in those of unsound nerves the state endureth only so long as would take to snap a finger; in some it endureth as long as the time taken for the eating of a meal; various treatises say the swoon endureth about three and one-half days, most others for four, during all which time the setting-face-to-face with the Clear Light ought to be persevered in. The symptoms are named as they come: now the symptoms of earth sinking into water are come. When all the symptoms of death are about to be completed, the dying one is enjoined with the great resolution: by taking advantage of this death, I will so act, for the good of all sentient beings peopling the illimitable expanse of the heavens, as to obtain Perfect Buddhahood, by resolving on love and compassion and by directing my entire effort to the Sole Perfection - and even if I cannot realize it, I will serve all sentient beings, infinite in number as are the limits of the sky.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the instruction is read aloud to the dying and, in hope, to the dead; a copy of the text - or strips of paper wound into a roll - is often tied to the corpse and burned or buried with it, as a Book of the Dead was entombed with a mummy.

functions: Liturgical technique of conscious dying: the text is read aloud, not studied silently, to a corpse or a dying person
Physiological doctrine of the death process as a reverse of the birth process, with the vital-force and median nerve mapped
Establishes the Great Perpendicular Path - instantaneous Buddhahood without further wandering - for the trained
Makes every funeral a re-enactment of the guru's teaching: whoever reads becomes the voice of the lineage

variants.name: The Ars Moriendi parallels
variants.text_tradition: European fifteenth-century death-manuals (Comper's edition, cited by Evans-Wentz)
variants.summary: Evans-Wentz compares the Tibetan reading-to-the-dying with the Christian Ars Moriendi, in which friends say prayers 'with a loud voice' before the dying - a structural parallel of both traditions' conviction that the dying moment decides the soul's fate.

variants.name: The Great Perfection (rDzogs-chen) recension
variants.summary: Those who have meditated on the Great Perfection and the Great Symbol recognize the Clear Light at the moment of death without the book being read; for all others the reading is indispensable.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Bardo Thodol remains a living liturgy read at Tibetan deathbeds and funerals to this day; passages below are paraphrases of the 1927 public-domain translation, never verbatim ritual text, and are given for study only.

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only, for study, not ritual use.

passages.text: O nobly-born, the time hath now come for thee to seek the Path in reality. Thy breathing is about to cease. Thy guru hath set thee face to face before with the Clear Light; and now thou art about to experience it in its Reality in the Bardo state, wherein all things are like the void and cloudless sky, and the naked, spotless intellect is like unto a transparent vacuum without circumference or centre. At this moment, know thou thyself; and abide in that state.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation, The Tibetan Book of the Dead (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: If the expiration is about to cease, turn the dying one over on the right side, the Lying Posture of a Lion; the throbbing of the arteries on the right and left side of the throat is to be pressed gently but firmly, whereby the vital-force will not be able to return from the median-nerve and will be sure to pass out through the Brahmanic aperture. At this moment the first glimpsing of the Bardo of the Clear Light of Reality, the Infallible Mind of the Dharma-Kaya, is experienced by all sentient beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The repetition of the address is to be persisted in until a yellowish liquid beginneth to appear from the apertures of the bodily organs; in those who have led an evil life, and in those of unsound nerves, the state endureth only so long as would take to snap a finger, and in some as long as the eating of a meal. When all the symptoms of death are about to be completed, the dying one is enjoined: by taking advantage of this death, I will so act, for the good of all sentient beings peopling the illimitable expanse of the heavens, as to obtain Perfect Buddhahood, by resolving on love and compassion - and even if I cannot realize it, I will serve all sentient beings, infinite in number as are the limits of the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Secondary Clear Light and the Question 'Am I Dead?'

region.en: Death-room of the deceased, Tibet (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亡者停靈之室（象徵定位）

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: If the Primary Clear Light is not recognized, the Secondary Clear Light dawns somewhat more than a meal-time period after the expiration has ceased; according to one's good or bad karma the vital-force flows down the right or left nerve and goes out through any of the apertures, and there comes a lucid condition of the mind. The consciousness-principle, getting outside the body, asks itself: Am I dead, or am I not dead? It cannot determine; it sees its relatives as it had been used to seeing them, and even hears the wailings - the terrifying karmic illusions have not yet dawned.
summary.zh: 若未識根本明光，則呼氣絕後約一頓飯時，第二明光顯現；依善惡業力，命力經左右脈從諸竅而出，心得清明。神識出體，自問：「我死了嗎？還沒死嗎？」無法自決；它如生前般看見親眷，甚至聽見哭聲——而可怕的業力幻象尚未現前。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: If it be feared that the primary Clear Light hath not been recognized, then there is dawning upon the deceased that called the Secondary Clear Light, which dawneth in somewhat more than a meal-time period after that the expiration hath ceased. According to one's good or bad karma, the vital-force floweth down into either the right or left nerve and goeth out through any of the apertures of the body; then cometh a lucid condition of the mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the consciousness-principle getteth outside the body, it sayeth to itself: Am I dead, or am I not dead? It cannot determine. It seeth its relatives and connexions as it had been used to seeing them before; it even heareth the wailings. The terrifying karmic illusions have not yet dawned, nor have the frightful apparitions or experiences caused by the Lords of Death yet come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Bardos and the Secret of Recognition

region.en: The Chonyid Bardo of the departed (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亡者之「實相中陰」（象徵定位）

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: Now that death has come to all, the departed is told not to cling; the six bardos are enumerated - the womb-bardo, the dream-bardo, the bardo of ecstatic equilibrium, the bardo of the moment of death, the bardo of Reality, and the bardo of the inverse process of sangsaric existence - and the key verses are recited: 'may I recognize whatever visions appear as the reflex of mine own consciousness... may I know the apparitions to be of the nature of apparitions; and, at this all-important moment of opportunity, may I know the emanations of the Peaceful and Wrathful Deities to be mine own thought-forms.' The body now is the thought-body of propensities: sounds, lights and rays cannot harm it, for it is incapable of dying.
summary.zh: 既死之人當知：死亡人皆有之，毋須戀棧。六中陰依次列舉——胎中、夢境、禪定、臨終、實相、受生——並誦關鍵偈：「願我認得一切顯現皆自心之影……願我知其幻化本性；於此大事因緣之際，願我知寂忿諸尊皆是自身心念之化現。」今之身乃「習氣意生身」，聲光影三相皆不能傷，以其本不能死。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: O nobly-born, that which is called death hath now come. Thou art departing from this world, but thou art not the only one; death cometh to all. Do not cling, in fondness and weakness, to this life. Even though thou clingest out of weakness, thou hast not the power to remain here; thou wilt gain nothing more than wandering in this Sangsara. Be not attached; be not weak. Remember the Precious Trinity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are six states of Bardo, namely: the natural state of Bardo while in the womb; the Bardo of the dream-state; the Bardo of ecstatic equilibrium while in deep meditation; the Bardo of the moment of death; the Bardo during the experiencing of Reality; and the Bardo of the inverse process of sangsaric existence - these are the six.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: When thy body and mind were separating, thou must have experienced a glimpse of the Pure Truth, subtle, sparkling, bright, dazzling, glorious, and radiantly awesome, in appearance like a mirage moving across a landscape in spring-time; be not daunted thereby, nor terrified, nor awed - that is the radiance of thine own true nature. From the midst of that radiance the natural sound of Reality, reverberating like a thousand thunders simultaneously sounding, will come; that is the natural sound of thine own real self. The body which thou hast now is called the thought-body of propensities; since thou hast not a material body of flesh and blood, whatever may come - sounds, lights or rays - are, all three, unable to harm thee; thou art incapable of dying. It is quite sufficient for thee to know that these apparitions are thine own thought-forms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Day: Vairochana and the Two Lights
title.zh: 中陰第一日：毗盧遮那與二光

region.en: The Central Realm, the Spreading Forth of the Seed (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中央密聚佛國（象徵定位）

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: Recovering from the three-and-a-half-day swoon, the departed sees the whole heavens deep blue; from the Central Realm called the Spreading Forth of the Seed the Bhagavan Vairochana, white, seated on a lion-throne, bearing an eight-spoked wheel, embraced by the Mother of the Space of Heaven, manifests. The blue light of the Wisdom of the Dharma-dhatu shoots forth from his heart - and beside it a dull white light from the devas: through the power of evil karma the glory produces fear and the dull light fondness, and the prayer is recited to be led by Vairochana across the fearful ambush of the Bardo into the state of All-Perfect Buddhahood in the Central Realm of the Densely-Packed.
summary.zh: 三日半昏沉初醒，所見長空盡作深藍；中央「遍佈種子」佛土，毗盧遮那白身獅座、手持八輻輪、與虛空佛母相擁而現。法界體性智之青光自其心間射出，耀不可視；同時一道灰白之光自天道而來。以惡業力故，青光反生怖畏，灰光反生貪戀——故誦祈請文，願毗盧遮那引度，越中陰險隘，譤於「密聚」中央佛國。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: As soon as thou art recovered from this swoon, thou wilt have the thought, what hath happened! Act so that thou wilt recognize the Bardo. At that time all the Sangsara will be in revolution, and the phenomenal appearances that thou wilt see then will be the radiances and deities; the whole heavens will appear deep blue. Then, from the Central Realm, called the Spreading Forth of the Seed, the Bhagavan Vairochana, white in colour, seated upon a lion-throne, bearing an eight-spoked wheel in his hand, and embraced by the Mother of the Space of Heaven, will manifest himself to thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wisdom of the Dharma-dhatu, blue in colour, shining, transparent, glorious, dazzling, from the heart of Vairochana as the Father-Mother will shoot forth and strike against thee with a light so radiant that thou wilt scarcely be able to look at it; and along with it there will also shine a dull white light from the devas. Because of the power of bad karma the glorious blue light will produce in thee fear and terror, and thou wilt wish to flee from it, and wilt beget a fondness for the dull white light of the devas - be not awed by the divine blue light, for that is the light of the Tathagata, and put thy whole thought earnestly upon Vairochana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Second Day: Vajra-Sattva and the Smoke of Hell
title.zh: 中陰第二日：金剛薩埵與獄火之煙

region.en: The Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東方喜吉祥佛國（象徵定位）

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: On the Second Day the pure form of water shines as a white light; from the Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness the Bhagavan Akshobhya as Vajra-Sattva, blue, holding a five-pronged vajra, on an elephant-throne, embraced by the Mother Mamaki, appears attended by the Bodhisattvas Kshitigarbha and Maitreya with the female Bodhisattvas Lasya and Puspa. The Mirror-like Wisdom shines as a bright radiant white light from the heart of Vajra-Sattva the Father-Mother - and a dull smoke-coloured light from Hell shines alongside: if the departed is attracted by it, he falls into the Hell-Worlds, whence there is no certain time of getting out.
summary.zh: 第二日，水大淨相現為白光；東方喜吉祥佛土，阿閦佛現金剛薩埵相——藍身、持五股杵、象座、與佛眼佛母（Mamaki）相擁，地藏與彌勒二菩薩及金剛鬘、蓮花二明妃隨侍。大圓鏡智之皎白光明自其心間射出——而地獄之暗煙色光並現：若貪之，即墮地獄，出期無定。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: On the Second Day the pure form of water will shine as a white light; at that time, from the deep blue Eastern Realm of Pre-eminent Happiness, the Bhagavan Akshobhya as Vajra-Sattva, blue in colour, holding in his hand a five-pronged vajra, seated upon an elephant-throne, and embraced by the Mother Mamaki, will appear to thee, attended by the Bodhisattvas Kshitigarbha and Maitreya with the female Bodhisattvas Lasya and Puspa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aggregate of thy principle of consciousness, being in its pure form - which is the Mirror-like Wisdom - will shine as a bright, radiant white light from the heart of Vajra-Sattva the Father-Mother, with such dazzling brilliancy that thou wilt scarcely be able to look at it; and a dull, smoke-coloured light from Hell will shine alongside. Through the power of anger thou wilt be startled at the dazzling white light and beget a fondness for the dull smoke-coloured light from Hell: if thou be attracted by it, thou wilt fall into the Hell-Worlds and endure unbearable misery, whence there is no certain time of getting out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Third Day: Ratna-Sambhava and the Light of Equality
title.zh: 中陰第三日：寶生佛與平等性智

region.en: The Southern Realm Endowed with Glory (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南方吉祥佛國（象徵定位）

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book I

summary.en: On the Third Day the primal form of the element earth shines as a yellow light; from the Southern Realm Endowed with Glory the Bhagavan Ratna-Sambhava, yellow, bearing a jewel, seated on a horse-throne and embraced by the Divine Mother Sangya-Chanmat, shines upon the departed, attended by Akasha-Garbha and Samanta-Bhadra with Mahiama and Dhupema. The Wisdom of Equality, dazzlingly yellow with satellite orbs of radiance, strikes against the departed - and beside it the dull bluish-yellow light of the human world path, of miserliness and greed.
summary.zh: 第三日，地大淨相現為黃光；南方吉祥佛土，寶生佛黃身持寶、馬座、與聖母相擁，虛空藏與普賢二菩薩及二明妃隨侍。平等性智之明黃光，帶光暈圍繞，射向亡者——旁有灰黃之倖光，即慳吝貪欲所致人道之光。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: On the Third Day the primal form of the element earth will shine forth as a yellow light; at that time, from the Southern Realm Endowed with Glory, the Bhagavan Ratna-Sambhava, yellow in colour, bearing a jewel in his hand, seated upon a horse-throne and embraced by the Divine Mother, will shine upon thee, attended by the Bodhisattvas Akasha-Garbha and Samanta-Bhadra with the two female Bodhisattvas, all in Buddha-form, coming to shine from amidst a rainbow halo of light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aggregate of touch in its primal form, as the yellow light of the Wisdom of Equality, dazzlingly yellow, glorified with orbs having satellite orbs of radiance, so clear and bright that the eye can scarcely look upon it, will strike against thee - and side by side with it the dull yellow light of the human world, the path of miserliness and greed, will shine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: The Blood-Drinking Herukas: The Wrathful Days

region.en: The Chonyid Bardo, quarters of the departed's brain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 實相中陰腦宮四方（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bardo Thodol (Bar-do thos-grol, terma attributed to Padmasambhava); English translation by Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz, 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (Oxford University Press, 1927), Part I, Book I: the eighth to fourteenth days

texts.license: Public domain (English translation published 1927; US public domain since 2023)

summary.en: On the eighth to fourteenth days the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities dawn - only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect, issuing from the quarters of the departed's own brain. The Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown, with three faces, six hands and four feet, nine eyes in terrifying gaze, eyebrows quivering like lightning, hair of reddish-yellow standing on end, garlanded with black serpents and raw human heads, holding wheel, sword and battle-axe, bell, skull-bowl and ploughshare, embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima who puts to his mouth a red shell filled with blood, comes forth from the departed's own brain - fear it not, for in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana the Father-Mother. Recognition is more difficult, but the intellect, undistractedly alert in one-pointedness under terror, is readier to be liberated - and the least of tantrika devotees will greet the blood-drinkers as tutelary deities, like human acquaintances.
summary.zh: 第八至十四日，五十八尊焰鬘熾燃、忿怒飲血之尊次第現前——彼即前七日寂靜諸尊之變相，自亡者腦宮四方而出。大悲赫魯迦深棕色，三面六臂四足，九目怒視，眉如電顫，赤黃髮豎，頸飾黑蛇與新剝人首為鬘，右手持輪、劍、斧，左手持鈴、顱器、犁鏵，佛母克羅提沙烏利瑪擁之，以盈血赤螺就其口——勿懼！其實即毗盧遮那父母雙運。此期怖畏更甚，然心因懼而專一，反易得度；最下之密乘行者亦能認彼為本尊，如遇故人。

texts.canonical_translation: Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, English translation; ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Tibetan Book of the Dead, Oxford 1927 (public domain)

narrative.en:
In the Bardo of the Peaceful Deities there were seven stages of ambuscade, and multitudes obtain liberation by recognition at one or another stage; but the number of sentient beings being great, evil karma powerful, obscurations dense, and propensities of too long standing, the Wheel of Ignorance and Illusion becometh neither exhausted nor accelerated, and there is a vast preponderance of those who wander downwards unliberated. Therefore, after the cessation of the dawning of the Peaceful and the Knowledge-Holding Deities, who come to welcome one, the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities come to dawn, who are only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect - according to the place of the thought-body of the deceased whence they proceed; nevertheless they will not resemble them.

This is the Bardo of the Wrathful Deities; and they being influenced by fear, terror and awe, recognition becometh more difficult; the intellect, gaining not in independence, passeth from one fainting state to a round of fainting states. Yet if one but recognize a little it is easier to be liberated at this stage - because of the dawning of the radiances, which produce fear, terror and awe, the intellect is undistractedly alert in one-pointedness. If at this stage one do not meet with this kind of teaching, one's hearing of religious lore, although it be like an ocean in its vastness, is of no avail; there are even discipline-holding abbots and doctors in metaphysical discourses who err at this stage, and, not recognizing, wander into the Sangsara. As for the common worldly folk, by fleeing through fear, terror and awe, they fall over the precipices into the unhappy worlds and suffer; but the least of the devotees of the mystic doctrines, as soon as he sees these blood-drinking deities, will recognize them to be his tutelary deities, and the meeting will be like that of human acquaintances - he will trust them, and becoming merged into them, in at-one-ment, will obtain Buddhahood.

O nobly-born, the Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown of colour, with three heads, six hands and four feet firmly postured; the right face being white, the left red, the central dark-brown; the body emitting flames of radiance; the nine eyes widely opened in terrifying gaze; the eyebrows quivering like lightning; the protruding teeth glistening and set over one another; giving vent to sonorous utterances of 'a-la-la' and 'ha-ha' and piercing whistling sounds; the hair of a reddish-yellow colour standing on end and emitting radiance; the heads adorned with dried human skulls and the symbols of the sun and moon; black serpents and raw human heads forming a garland for the body; the first of the right hands holding a wheel, the middle one a sword, the last one a battle-axe; the first of the left hands a bell, the middle one a skull-bowl, the last one a ploughshare; his body embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima, her right hand clinging to his neck and her left putting to his mouth a red shell filled with blood - these two deities together will come forth from within thine own brain and shine vividly upon thee. Fear that not. Be not awed. Know it to be the embodiment of thine own intellect. As it is thine own tutelary deity, be not terrified; in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana, the Father-Mother. Simultaneously with the recognition, liberation will be obtained.

If one flee from them, then on the Ninth Day the blood-drinking deities of the Vajra Order named the Bhagavan Vajra-Heruka, dark-blue, issue from the eastern quarter of the brain; on the Tenth Day the blood-drinking deity of the Precious-Gem Order named Ratna-Heruka, yellow, issues from the southern quarter; on the Eleventh Day the blood-drinking deity of the Lotus Order, Padma-Heruka, reddish-black, from the western quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amitabha; on the Twelfth Day the blood-drinking deity of the Karmic Order, Karma-Heruka, dark green, accompanied by the Kerima, Htamenaa and Wang-chugma, from the northern quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amoghasiddhi. Each time the address repeats: fear not, be not terrified, be not awed, know them to be the embodiment of thine own intellect, and Buddhahood will be obtained by merging in them in at-one-ment.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the wrathful sequence inverts ordinary terror into liberation - the most frightful forms are the closest to home, one's own brain and one's own tutelary deities - which is why the practitioner meditates on their images while alive. The blood symbolizes sangsaric existence; 'blood-drinking' the thirsting for, and quenching of, the thirst for existence.

functions: Inverts the terror of the death-visions into the path: the more frightful the apparition, the closer to one's own mind
Grounds iconographic practice: seeing the painted likenesses and images while alive secures recognition at death
Democratizes the liberation doctrine: the least of tantrika devotees meets the blood-drinkers like old acquaintances
Explains the funeral signs - rainbow-halo and bone-reliques - as the residue of esoteric recognition

variants.name: The 58 blood-drinking deities in the mandala paintings
variants.text_tradition: The Great Mandala of the Knowledge-Holding and Wrathful Deities (folio paintings reproduced in Evans-Wentz)
variants.summary: The painted mandalas show the united manifestation of the Wrathful Deities, the three-headed Herukas of the five orders at the cruciform design's centre, and the King and Judge of the Dead, Shinje, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara, weighing the dead.

variants.name: The Great Symbol (Mahamudra) schools
variants.summary: Devotees of the Great Symbol and the Great Perfection recognize the Clear Light at the moment of death and do not need the reading of the Thodol; they may obtain the Sambhoga-Kaya in the Chonyid Bardo or the Nirmana-Kaya in the Sidpa Bardo.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The wrathful deities are living liturgical images, painted and meditated in Tibetan monasteries; passages below are paraphrases of the 1927 public-domain translation for study, not for ritual use, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: After the cessation of the dawning of the Peaceful and the Knowledge-Holding Deities, the fifty-eight flame-enhaloed, wrathful, blood-drinking deities come to dawn, who are only the former Peaceful Deities in changed aspect; this is the Bardo of the Wrathful Deities, and they being influenced by fear, terror and awe, recognition becometh more difficult - yet if one but recognize a little, it is easier to be liberated at this stage, because the intellect is undistractedly alert in one-pointedness under terror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Great Glorious Buddha-Heruka, dark-brown, with three heads, six hands and four feet firmly postured, the nine eyes widely opened in terrifying gaze, the eyebrows quivering like lightning, the hair of reddish-yellow standing on end, the heads adorned with dried human skulls and the symbols of the sun and moon, black serpents and raw human heads forming a garland for the body, his body embraced by the Mother Buddha-Krotishaurima, her right hand clinging to his neck and her left putting to his mouth a red shell filled with blood - these two deities together will come forth from within thine own brain and shine vividly upon thee: fear that not, know it to be the embodiment of thine own intellect; in reality it is the Bhagavan Vairochana, the Father-Mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the Ninth Day the blood-drinking Vajra-Heruka, dark-blue, issues from the eastern quarter of thy brain - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Vajra-Sattva; on the Tenth Day Ratna-Heruka, yellow, from the southern quarter; on the Eleventh Day Padma-Heruka, reddish-black, from the western quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amitabha; and on the Twelfth Day Karma-Heruka, dark green, from the northern quarter - in reality the Father-Mother Bhagavan Amoghasiddhi. Each time: fear not, be not terrified, be not awed, know them to be the embodiment of thine own intellect, and Buddhahood will be obtained by merging in them in at-one-ment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: Shinje, King and Judge of the Dead

region.en: Court of the Judge of the Dead in the Bardo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中陰閻羅法庭（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bardo Thodol tradition (mandala text and iconography); English ed. Evans-Wentz 1927

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (1927), Introduction, the Judgement Scene

summary.en: Shinje - the King and Judge of the Dead, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara, monkey-headed - presides over the weighing: on one side heaped-up black pebbles, the evil deeds, on the other white pebbles, the good deeds; the Little White God empties a sack of white pebbles, the Little Black God a sack of black, and guarding the weighing stand the buffalo-headed officers; from the court issue the six paths, bearing the recently judged - a scene Evans-Wentz sets beside the judgement in the tenth book of Plato's Republic, where the just ascend by the heavenly way on the right and the unjust descend on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
summary.zh: 閻魔王（辛傑）——觀音之忿怒相、猴面之王——主持稱量：一側堆黑石為惡業，一側堆白石為善業；白神傾倒善石之袋，黑神傾倒惡石之袋，牛頭獄卒守秤；六道之門自法庭兩側而出，剛受審判者列隊其間——伊文思溫茲將此景與柏拉圖《理想國》第十卷之審判並觀：善者由右天路上升，惡者由左下道而降，背上縛其業跡。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 edition only.

passages.text: Shinje is the King and Judge of the Dead, the wrathful aspect of Avalokiteshvara; in the Judgement Scene there is the symbolical weighing - before him, on one side, heaped-up black pebbles, the evil deeds, and on the other heaped-up white pebbles, the good deeds. On the right of Shinje stands the Little White God, emptying a sack of white pebbles; on the other side the Little Black God, emptying a sack of black pebbles; and guarding the weighing are the buffalo-headed officers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927), Introduction; not verbatim.

passages.text: Issuing from the Court, on either side of the Judge, are the six paths, and on them are seated twelve of the dead who have recently been judged - a scene closely resembling the Judgement described in the tenth book of Plato's Republic, where judges seated in the intermediate space commanded the just, after judgement, to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and the unjust to descend by the lower way on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927) quoting Jowett's Plato; not verbatim.

region.en: The Sidpa Bardo of the wanderer (symbolic pin)

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, trans. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup, ed. Evans-Wentz (1927), Book II

summary.en: In the Sidpa Bardo the wanderer, having failed recognition, undergoes visions of the Judgment of the Lords of Death - who number all deeds with the mirror and the scales of black and white pebbles - then wanders pursued by karmic winds, seeking a womb; the methods of closing the doors of the womb, the choosing of the place of birth, and the reading of omens of the sex and caste of the coming life follow, the consciousness-principle drinking of forgetfulness as it enters the door of the womb.
summary.zh: 受生中陰中，未得認識之亡者將見閻魔王之審判——以鏡與黑白石之秤算盡其業——復為業風所逐，尋求投生之胎；經中遂教以關閉胎門之法、擇生之方，以及觀察來生性別種姓之兆，神識飲忘川之水而入胎門。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1927 translation only.

passages.text: Now henceforth thou art going to experience the other two, the Chonyid Bardo and the Sidpa Bardo. In the Sidpa Bardo, having failed to recognize the visions of the Peaceful and the Wrathful Deities as thine own thought-forms, thou wilt wander, subject to the karmic winds, until the place of rebirth is found - and the teachings, therefore, go on to the methods of closing the doors of the womb while in the Intermediate State when seeking rebirth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup's translation (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: Drinking of the River of Forgetfulness, the consciousness-principle enters the door of the womb and is reborn direct from the desire-world called the Sidpa Bardo - the lower rebirth being unendowed, because of the lack of enlightenment of the one undergoing it, with consciousness of the process.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.

title.en: Er the Pamphylian and the Ch choosing of Bodies
title.zh: 珀菲里亞人之厄爾與擇生

region.en: The otherworld of Plato's Republic, compared by Evans-Wentz (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柏拉圖《理想國》之他世（伊文思溫茲並觀，象徵定位）

texts.period: Plato, Republic, Bk. X (4th century BC), compared by Evans-Wentz 1927 with the Sidpa Bardo

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (1927), Introduction, quoting Plato's Republic, Bk. X

summary.en: Evans-Wentz's great cross-cultural comparison: Er, son of Armenius, slain in battle, found uncorrupted, returned to life on the funeral pile on the twelfth day and told what he had seen - a mysterious place with two openings in the earth and two in the heaven, judges seated in the intermediate space, the just ascending by the heavenly way on the right and the unjust descending on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds - and then the choosing of lives: Orpheus taking the swan, Ajax the lion, Agamemnon the eagle, Atalanta the athlete, Epeius the cunning woman, Therites the monkey, and Odysseus, disabused of ambition, the neglected life of a private man who had no cares.
summary.zh: 伊文思溫茲的大跨文化對照：厄爾戰歿而屍身不腐，第十二日於火葬堆上復生，述其所見——地有二口、天有二口之秘境，中間坐著審判者，善者由右天路而升，惡者由左下道而降，背縛其業跡；繼而眾魂擇生：奧菲斯取天鵝，埃阿斯取獅，阿伽門農取鷹，阿塔蘭忒取力士，厄珀俄斯取巧女，特西忒斯取猿——而厭倦了野心的奧德修斯，取那被眾人遺忘的「無憂平民之生」。

sensitivity.note: Comparative material from Evans-Wentz's edition; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth, was slain in battle, and ten days afterwards, when the bodies of the dead were taken up already in a state of corruption, his body was found unaffected by decay, and carried home to be buried; and on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, he returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left the body he went on a journey with a great company, and they came to a mysterious place at which there were two openings in the earth, and over against them two other openings in the heaven above; in the intermediate space there were judges seated, who commanded the just, after they had given judgement on them, to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and the unjust to descend by the lower way on the left, these also bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most curious was the spectacle - sad and laughable and strange; for the choice of the souls was in most cases based on their own experience of a previous life: the soul which had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan out of enmity to the race of women; Ajax refusing to be a man, remembering the injustice done him in the judgement about the arms, chose the life of a lion; Agamemnon took the life of an eagle; Atalanta, seeing the great fame of an athlete, was unable to resist the temptation; Epeius passed into the nature of a woman cunning in the arts; the jester Therites was putting on the form of a monkey - and Odysseus, the mutabilities of human life having disabused him of ambition, went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares, and, finding it lying about and neglected by everybody else, said he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last, and was delighted to have it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.
